input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a well-established technique for recovering valuable or unwanted solutes from liquid streams, and in the present case it is to be used to recover acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, which expresses the ratio between the concentration of the solute in the organic phase and its concentration in the aqueous phase, is 0.91 at 25 °C for this system, and the design that has been developed on this basis makes use of 8 countercurrent stages. On the basis of these figures, the predicted recovery is 91% of the acetone in the feed, which represents a substantial proportion of the material to be recovered. The practical consequence of a coefficient of this size is that the solvent has to do its work over a number of successive contacts rather than in a single equilibrium stage, which is why a multi-stage countercurrent arrangement has been adopted for the separation. It should be noted, however, that this prediction rests on a number of assumptions, in particular the assumption that every stage behaves as an equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two phases is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents that are to be used, and so the recovery figure should be understood as a prediction that is conditional on the behaviour of the real system, which may well depart from the idealised behaviour that has been assumed in arriving at it.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the concentration of acetone in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium, is 0.91 at 25 °C. A coefficient below unity means that at equilibrium the aqueous phase holds more acetone per unit volume than the organic phase takes up, so a single contact leaves most of the acetone behind; recovery is built up over stages instead. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages, in which the phases pass in opposite directions and the leanest solvent meets the most depleted aqueous stream. Countercurrent flow keeps a concentration difference alive along the whole cascade: at every stage the aqueous phase meets solvent that has taken up less acetone than the solvent it met at the stage before, so transfer continues even as the aqueous stream is depleted. Predicted recovery is 91% of the acetone in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages, with the phases leaving each stage in equilibrium at the stated coefficient, and negligible mutual solubility, with each phase keeping its own volume through the cascade. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The recovery therefore stands as a design estimate: if the phases fall short of equilibrium on each stage, or dissolve into each other enough to move material between them, the recovery achieved will fall below the predicted figure, and the size of the shortfall is not known until the solvents are tested. The estimate is nevertheless the design basis as it stands, and the stage count of the design has been fixed from it.
